highlights: The Diet extended its session to debate the draft constitution, focusing on popular sovereignty, imperial prerogatives, and the renunciation of war.
Severe food shortages forced SCAP to release 174,708 metric tons of imported cereals and canned goods to 20 deficit prefectures.
At the IMTFE, eyewitnesses including Dr. Robert Wilson and Miner Searle Bates provided harrowing testimony on the 1937 Rape of Nanking.
Screening under the 4 January Purge Directive was substantially completed, barring prominent figures including Mitsu Kono and Haruo Matsui from public office.
Violent armed clashes between rival black-market gangs and police in Tokyo's Shibuya and Shimbashi districts left six dead, prompting stall shutdowns.
The Board of Communications was elevated to the Ministry of Communications on 1 July, with Sadakichi Hitotsumatsu installed as minister.
The first shipments of American raw cotton totaling 30,000 bales arrived in Japanese mills to begin manufacturing textiles for export.

sections.title: Front matter

sections.summary: Monthly summary of political, economic, and social developments in Japan during July 1946.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: Under SCAP General Orders No. 30 on 26 July, the Office of Civilian Personnel was discontinued as a special staff section and its functions assumed by USAFPAC.
sections.title: Organization under SCAP

sections.summary: The Diet debated the draft constitution, focusing on popular sovereignty and the Emperor. The government substantially completed screening officials under the Purge Directive, while the Social Democrats rejected communist collaboration.
sections.title: Political Activities

sections.summary: Finance Minister Ishibashi outlined a recovery program emphasizing coal and fertilizer. Critical staple food shortages forced emergency releases of imported foodstuffs to 20 prefectures, while note circulation expanded rapidly.
sections.title: Economic Activities

sections.summary: Public assistance aided 2.19 million people, while cholera outbreaks occurred in Fukuyama and Yokosuka. The Ministry of Education established Citizens' Public Halls for adult education and banned deleted wartime textbooks starting 1 August.
sections.title: Social Activities

sections.summary: Political developments, public safety, legal reforms, and war crimes prosecution during July 1946.
sections.title: Part II: Political

sections.summary: The Diet extended its session to 28 August to deliberate the draft constitution and Ishibashi's economic policies. Screening under the Purge Directive removed prominent figures like Mitsu Kono, and the Board of Communications became a ministry.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Clashes between rival black-market gangs in Shibuya and Shimbashi resulted in gun battles, prompting police shutdowns of open-air stalls. Tokyo crime nearly doubled since January, and a major fire destroyed 400 houses in Iida.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: SCAP ordered 65 suspected war criminals apprehended, while the IMTFE heard testimony on the 1928 assassination of Chang Tso-lin and Japanese atrocities during the Rape of Nanking. General Myron C. Cramer replaced Justice Higgins on the Tribunal.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Economic developments in industry, agriculture, commerce, finance, and resources during July 1946.
sections.title: Part III: Economic

sections.summary: Crop forecasts indicated improved 1946 harvests despite poor wheat and barley yields. June fish landings dropped due to the close of Hokkaido's herring season, while 263 newly converted fishing vessels operated by late July.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: Coal production reached 1.66 million metric tons in June, but severe shortages hampered metallurgy and chemicals. Seventeen of 25 tracked minerals increased output in May, while Imperial Oil struggled with high costs.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: To conserve coal, iron and steel production was concentrated at the Yawata plant. June chemical output met only 32 percent of minimum needs, while 12 steel ships and four launched vessels were completed.
sections.title: Heavy Industries

sections.summary: Machine tool production fell as manufacturers feared reparations, but truck chassis output rose to 1,483 units in June. Food processing fluctuated seasonally, and watch and clock manufacturing steadily expanded to 62,193 units.
sections.title: Manufacturing

sections.summary: First imports of American raw cotton totaling 30,000 bales arrived for export yarn production. Raw silk output dropped slightly due to coal and food shortages, while rayon pulp output tripled.
sections.title: Textile Industries

sections.summary: Rail freight decreased to 8.14 million tons in June, and coal shortages left 72.5 percent of gas manufacturing capacity idle. Electric power generation remained adequate with the completion of the Nagamatsu hydroelectric plant.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: The Board of Communications was elevated to ministry status on 1 July, and mail rates rose 200 percent. Critical shortages of vacuum tubes persisted, while long-distance telephone service was expanded for Occupation Forces.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: The Labor Disputes Adjustment Bill was submitted to the Diet amid union protests. Government workers secured a 50 percent wage increase, while SCAP established a 40-hour work week and paid leave for Occupation-employed laborers.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: Commercial imports surged in July with 50 ships delivering 326,000 tons of goods, primarily food, cotton, and phosphate. Exports included coal to Hong Kong and Korea, alongside shipments of raw silk and metals to the United States.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: A severe staple food crisis forced SCAP to release 174,708 tons of imported cereals and canned foods across 20 prefectures. Vegetable deliveries to urban legal markets plummeted after subsidies were removed.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note circulation climbed to ¥47.23 billion by 20 July due to government deficit financing. SCAP permitted the dissolution of the Yokohama Specie Bank and reviewed proposed national tax revisions.
sections.title: Finance

sections.summary: SCAP approved articles for the Holding Company Liquidation Commission, restricted additional concerns including Titan Industrial, and revised the interim reparations list by deleting 60 plants and adding 21. Blocked precious metals were analyzed.
sections.title: Property Control and Reparations

sections.summary: Public health, welfare, education, religion, and information media activities during July 1946.
sections.title: Part IV: Social

sections.summary: Cholera outbreaks in Hiroshima and Kanagawa Prefectures were brought under control, while typhus incidence fell sharply. Nutrition surveys revealed an average daily intake of only 1,352 calories in Tokyo, and 524,005 Japanese repatriated.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: The Ministry of Education initiated Citizens' Public Halls, reinstated geography instruction with new textbooks, and screened teachers in Chiba. The Japan Newspaper Publishers and Editors Association adopted democratic canons of journalism.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

summary: Summation No. 10 covers non-military activities in Japan during July 1946, a critical transitional month marked by severe food shortages and historic institutional reforms. The report documents the acute food crisis that forced SCAP to release over 174,000 metric tons of imported cereals and canned goods across 20 deficit prefectures to prevent widespread starvation. In the Diet, intense debates centered on the draft constitution, particularly the concepts of popular sovereignty, the symbolic status of the Emperor, and the renunciation of war. Concurrently, the government substantially completed the purge of militarists from public office and established the Ministry of Communications. In the economic realm, coal shortages severely curtailed industrial output, prompting the concentration of all steelmaking at Yawata, while the arrival of the first 30,000 bales of American raw cotton began revitalizing the export textile sector. At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, prosecution witnesses provided harrowing eyewitness testimony regarding the Mukden Incident and the Rape of Nanking. For historians, this issue provides invaluable empirical data on May nutrition surveys, black-market gang warfare in Tokyo, labor union reorganization, and early Occupation governance.
